You want to start another language course at the adult education center, but first need a placement test. Write a letter and ask for an appointment.

1. Reason for your letter
2. Which language you want to learn
3. Why this is important to you
4. When you would have time for the test

parts.en: Essen, 6 May 2026
Dear Sir or Madam,
<r>I am writing to you because</r> I have been thinking about starting another language course for a long time, and now I would finally like to do it.
<r>I would like to</r> learn English, because of my new job, since English is mainly spoken there.
<r>This matters to me because</r> I would like to have more confidence in conversations with my colleagues, and that would help me a lot.
<r>I would prefer</r> the next available appointment this week. I'm also available almost every afternoon.
<r>I look forward to your reply.</r>
Best regards,
Mark Fischer

task.en:
You recently mastered a big challenge (for example, completed a German course). A person supported you through it. Write her an email.

1. Reason for your email
2. What kind of challenge it was
3. How you managed it
4. Thanks for the support

parts.en: Subject: I did it!
Dear Sabine,
<r>I had to write to you right away that</r> I have finally completed my German course. I didn't give up until I had really reached my goal.
<r>More specifically,</r> the hardest part was continuing every day, even though I sometimes wanted to give up.
<r>I managed it because</r> persevering mattered more to me than giving up, and I never lost sight of my goal.
<r>I therefore want to thank you</r> very much for your support, because without you I wouldn't have managed it.
<r>I am so proud, and I owe that to you too!</r>
Lots of love,
Anna Vogel

task.en:
You are taking part in an integration counseling program. Your counselor would like to know how you are doing. Write him a letter about your everyday life.

1. Reason for your letter
2. What your daily life currently looks like
3. What is still difficult for you
4. A request for advice

parts.en: Hanover, 11 February 2026
Dear Mr. Wolf,
<r>I am writing to you because</r> you wanted to know how I am doing, and I would like to briefly tell you about my everyday life and getting settled here.
<r>My day usually starts early,</r> I work at the office until the afternoon, and after that I still go shopping.
<r>What is still difficult for me is</r> that, even though I already feel at home here, understanding certain conversations at government offices is hard.
<r>I would be grateful if</r> you could give me some advice about that. I would also welcome a personal conversation.
<r>Thank you in advance for your help.</r>
Best regards,
David Berger

task.en:
There was recently a misunderstanding between you and a colleague that annoyed you. You want to clear it up. Write him an email.

1. Reason for your email
2. What annoyed you
3. How the misunderstanding happened
4. A suggestion for how to clear it up

parts.en: Subject: Let's quickly clear this up
Hi Ben,
<r>I have to be honest,</r> I was quite annoyed about that because of the misunderstanding, and I would like to clear it up.
<r>More specifically,</r> I was annoyed that you said nothing in the meeting, even though you had told my colleague exactly about it.
<r>I think</r> someone misunderstood our conversation and then passed it on incorrectly.
<r>Let's just have a quick phone call</r> to sort everything out calmly. Then we can quickly get this out of the way.
<r>I'm sure this will be sorted out quickly.</r>
Take care,
Nina Falk

task.en:
You have been invited to a family celebration and don't yet know the local customs exactly. Write a letter to a colleague and ask for tips.

1. Reason for your letter
2. What you are invited to
3. What you don't know
4. A request for advice on etiquette

parts.en: Mainz, 30 September 2026
Dear Petra,
<r>I have a favor to ask you</r>, because I'm still unsure about the local customs here, what's typical and what isn't.
<r>I've actually been invited to</r> a family celebration, and I don't want to do anything wrong there.
<r>For example, I don't know</r> what I should pay attention to when greeting people, because I don't want to offend anyone.
<r>I would be grateful for</r> a few tips that I can rely on. I would also welcome a short conversation beforehand.
<r>Thanks in advance for your help.</r>
Take care,
Alex Berg

task.en:
You were briefly in the hospital due to an accident, but you are already feeling better. Write an email to a friend.

1. Reason for your email
2. What happened
3. How you are feeling now
4. An invitation for her to visit you in the hospital

parts.en: Subject: Don't worry, I'm already feeling better!
Dear Katja,
<r>I have to quickly tell you that</r> I had a small accident two days ago, and was therefore briefly in the emergency room.
<r>More specifically,</r> I fell off my bike after I had ridden over a stone.
<r>Luckily I'm already feeling better,</r> because the injury was fortunately not dangerous.
<r>I would be very happy if</r> you could come visit me here. The visiting hours are also quite flexible.
<r>See you soon, I'm already looking forward to it!</r>
Lots of love,
Julia Neumann

task.en:
You had an examination at the hospital last week, but you have not yet received the results. Write an email to the hospital.

1. Reason for your email
2. When the examination was
3. Why the results matter to you
4. A request for quick delivery

parts.en: Subject: Results of my examination from last Monday
Dear Sir or Madam,
<r>I am writing to you because</r> I have not yet received my test results, even though they will certainly be available by now.
<r>As a reminder:</r> the examination was on Monday last week, and I had been promised that I would get the results after a few days.
<r>This matters to me because</r> my further recovery depends on the diagnosis, and I want to start therapy as soon as possible.
<r>I therefore ask you to</r> send me the results as soon as possible. A brief phone call would also be helpful.
<r>Thank you for your prompt handling.</r>
Best regards,
Mark Fischer

task.en:
You recently helped during an emergency in your neighborhood. You would like to know how the person is doing now. Write a letter to the family.

1. Reason for your letter
2. What happened during the emergency
3. What you did
4. A request for news about their health

parts.en: Bonn, 17 March 2026
Dear Sabine,
<r>I wanted to write to you because</r> I would not only like to know how your father is doing, but also because the emergency is still on my mind.
<r>As far as I know,</r> your father suddenly collapsed, and he must have lost consciousness.
<r>I immediately</r> called the ambulance and waited with him until it arrived.
<r>I would be grateful if</r> you could let me know briefly. I would be very happy about that. I would also like to know if there is anything else I can do.
<r>I'm thinking of you all.</r>
With love,
Anna Vogel

topic.en: Long waiting time at the emergency room

task.en:
You recently had to wait a very long time for treatment at the emergency room, even though your case was urgent. Write an email to the hospital administration.

1. Reason for your email
2. How long you had to wait
3. Why this was a problem for you
4. A suggestion for improvement

parts.en: Subject: Long waiting time at the emergency room
Dear Sir or Madam,
<r>I am writing to you</r> to complain about the long waiting time in your emergency room.
<r>More specifically,</r> despite urgent complaints I had to wait more than three hours, even though I had immediately submitted the completed form.
<r>This was a big problem for me because</r> the urgency of my case was obviously not recognized, and my condition even worsened during that time.
<r>I therefore suggest</r> that the priority of patients should be assessed better. A clear update on the waiting time would also be helpful.
<r>I hope for a serious review of my concern.</r>
Best regards,
David Berger

task.en:
You will soon have to undergo surgery and will therefore be absent for a longer period. Write a letter to your employer.

1. Reason for your letter
2. When the surgery takes place
3. How long you will be absent, approximately
4. A request for understanding

parts.en: Duisburg, 25 January 2026
Dear Ms. Roth,
<r>I am writing to you because</r> I soon have to undergo surgery, so that you can plan in time.
<r>The surgery is</r> scheduled for the 14th of the month, and my surgeon has already explained all the details to me.
<r>I will probably be</r> absent for a few weeks, because the recovery time after such an operation is usually longer.
<r>I therefore ask you to</r> please have understanding for the fact that I will not be reachable during this time. I will also hand everything over properly beforehand.
<r>Thank you for your understanding.</r>
Best regards,
Nina Falk

task.en:
Your wife recently gave birth to your child at this hospital, and you would like to thank them for the good care. Write an email to the ward.

1. Reason for your email
2. What you particularly liked
3. Who took care of you
4. Thanks to the team

parts.en: Subject: Heartfelt thanks for the wonderful care
Dear maternity ward team,
<r>I am writing to you because</r> I would like to thank you for the safety and good care during the birth of our child, and I don't want that to go unmentioned.
<r>What I particularly liked was</r> how loving everyone was with us, and how clean everything was.
<r>There was one nurse</r> whom I would especially like to thank, because she took care of us the whole time.
<r>I therefore want to thank the whole team</r> for the best experience we could have wished for. I will also always recommend this hospital.
<r>Once again, heartfelt thanks from our whole family.</r>
Warm regards,
Alex Berg

topic.en: A swap event for the neighborhood

task.en:
You want to organize a swap event for used clothing with your neighbors in order to live more sustainably. Write an email to the neighbors.

1. Reason for your email
2. What exactly you are planning
3. Why this matters to you
4. A request for feedback

parts.en: Subject: Idea for a swap event
Dear neighbors,
<r>I wanted to write to you all because</r> sustainability in everyday life matters a lot to me, and I have an idea for all of us.
<r>I'm planning</r> to organize a small clothing swap event for used clothing, so that we throw away less and share more.
<r>This matters to me because</r> I want to change something because of the scarcity of resources, and together we can surely achieve more.
<r>I would be happy if</r> you could let me know briefly whether you're interested. You're also welcome to invite more neighbors.
<r>I look forward to your replies.</r>
Take care,
Julia Neumann

topic.en: Energy waste due to poor insulation

task.en:
A lot of energy is being wasted in your apartment because the windows are poorly insulated. Write an email to your landlord.

1. Reason for your email
2. What exactly the problem is
3. Since when you have noticed this
4. A suggestion for a solution

parts.en: Subject: Energy waste due to poor window insulation
Dear Mr. Bauer,
<r>I am writing to you because</r> a lot of energy is being wasted in my apartment.
<r>More specifically,</r> poorly insulated windows let a lot of warmth escape outside in winter, and that shows up clearly on the bill.
<r>I noticed this</r> since the heating costs rose sharply last winter.
<r>I therefore suggest</r> that the windows should be re-insulated. A solar panel on the roof would also be a good investment.
<r>I hope for a quick solution.</r>
Best regards,
Mark Fischer

topic.en: Accepting the invitation to the environmental day

task.en:
A friend invites you to an environmental day in your neighborhood (collecting litter, planting trees). Write her a letter.

1. Thanks for the invitation and your acceptance
2. Why environmental protection matters to you
3. What you would like to bring to the environmental day
4. A question about the time and meeting point

parts.en: Dresden, 5 September 2026
Dear Karin,
<r>Thank you so much for your invitation,</r> I was really delighted that you're planning an environmental day in our neighborhood, and of course I'll be very happy to join.
<r>This matters to me because</r> I've been interested in environmental protection for a long time and like to help out, so that our streets become cleaner.
<r>I'm planning</r> to bring some gloves and garbage bags, and I could also get a few small trees for the planting.
<r>I still have one question:</r> before the environmental day starts, when and where exactly are we meeting?
<r>I'm really looking forward to it.</r>
Take care,
Anna Vogel

topic.en: Invitation to the harvest festival at the organic farm

task.en:
Your organic farm is holding a harvest festival with seasonal vegetables and guided tours. You want to invite the neighborhood. Write a letter to the local residents.

1. Reason for your letter
2. When and where the festival takes place
3. What visitors can expect there
4. A request to register

parts.en: Freiburg, 20 August 2026
Dear Sir or Madam,
<r>I would like to warmly invite you to our harvest festival,</r> because this year, as part of marketing our seasonal produce, we're also offering exciting tours around the farm.
<r>The festival takes place on</r> Saturday, 12 September, from 2 pm at our farm, where you can also visit our animals. There will also be coffee and cake for all guests.
<r>With us you can see</r> how we organize the planting of new trees, and how our vegetables grow completely without artificial fertilizer.
<r>I would be very grateful if</r> you could register by 5 September, so that we can plan enough food and seating.
<r>I look forward to your visit.</r>
Best regards,
David Berger

task.en:
You had agreed to help your friend with the harvest on her farm, but the arranged appointment no longer suits you. Write her an email.

1. Reason for your email
2. Why the appointment no longer works
3. An alternative date suggestion
4. A request for a quick reply

parts.en: Subject: Our appointment for the harvest help
Hi Lea,
<r>I'm writing to you because</r> I unfortunately have to postpone our appointment for the harvest help, because a lot is currently being reorganized at my work.
<r>The appointment unfortunately no longer works for me,</r> even though I was really looking forward to the day, because I have to take extra shifts this weekend.
<r>I suggest</r> that we postpone the appointment to the weekend after next, because by then I'll have more time again.
<r>Could you please</r> let me know briefly whether the new date also works for you? You don't have to reply right away, but a short message would already be enough.
<r>I look forward to your reply.</r>
Take care,
Nina Falk

task.en:
There are still no separate bins for paper, glass and general waste in your building. You would like to change that. Write a letter to the property management.

1. Reason for your letter
2. Why this issue matters to you
3. A concrete suggestion
4. A request for a reply

parts.en: Hamburg, 2 September 2026
Dear Sir or Madam,
<r>I'm writing to you about</r> a problem that I've wanted to raise for a while: our building still doesn't have separate bins for paper, glass and general waste.
<r>This matters to me because</r> the topic of sustainability is very close to my heart, and each of us should do something about climate change.
<r>I suggest</r> that we put three separate bins in the courtyard, so that all residents can sort their waste properly. That would be a simple and inexpensive solution.
<r>I would be pleased</r> if you could briefly let me know what you think of my suggestion. I hope that we'll find a solution soon.
<r>Thank you in advance for your efforts.</r>
Best regards,
Alex Berg

task.en:
Your friend invited you to an art exhibition, but you can't make it. Write her an email.

1. Reason for your email
2. Why you can't attend
3. Apology and a suggestion for another date
4. Wish to meet up soon

parts.en: Subject: Unfortunately I have to cancel
Dear Mira,
<r>Thank you so much for your invitation to the</r> art exhibition, but I unfortunately have to cancel: I'm really happy about the invitation, but I already have another appointment that day.
<r>The reason for this is</r> that I had already arranged an important appointment beforehand, and I unfortunately can't change it anymore.
<r>I'm really sorry,</r> but if it worked for you, we could also visit the exhibition together next week.
<r>I hope</r> to see you again soon and I'm already really looking forward to our next get-together.
<r>See you soon!</r>
Take care,
Julia Neumann

topic.en: Accepting the invitation to the music festival

task.en:
Your friend invited you to a music festival that's already taking place in a week. Write him a letter.

1. Thanks for the invitation and your acceptance
2. How you're preparing for the festival
3. What you're most looking forward to
4. A question about the details (meeting point, what to bring)

parts.en: Cologne, 8 September 2026
Dear Tom,

explanation.en:
When you want to politely ask for something or ask a question, use Konjunktiv II instead of the normal present tense.
The two most common forms are könnten (from können) and würden (from werden) + infinitive at the end of the sentence.
Important: the main verb stays in the infinitive and goes right to the end.
Example: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen? (Could you please help me?) Würden Sie das Fenster schließen? (Would you close the window?)
Compare: Hilf mir! (a direct command) vs. Könnten Sie mir helfen? (polite)

rule.en:
Formation
For polite requests and questions we use the Konjunktiv II of the verbs können and werden.

Personkönnenwerden
ichkönntewürde
dukönntestwürdest
er/sie/eskönntewürde
wirkönntenwürden
ihrkönntetwürdet
sie/Siekönntenwürden

Word order
The modal verb takes position 2, the main verb (infinitive) goes to the end of the sentence.
Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?
Würden Sie das Fenster schließen?

Usage
This form sounds much friendlier than the imperative or the present tense.
Compare: Schließen Sie das Fenster! (direct) vs. Würden Sie das Fenster schließen? (polite)

explanation.en:
When a sentence has two verbs, they're often connected with zu + infinitive, placed at the end of the sentence.
This typically happens after expressions like Es ist wichtig, ... zu ..., Ich habe Lust, ... zu ..., or Ich versuche, ... zu ....
Careful with separable verbs: 'zu' slips between the prefix and the stem (einkaufen -> einzukaufen).
Example: Ich versuche, Deutsch zu lernen. (I'm trying to learn German.) Es ist schön, einzukaufen. (It's nice to go shopping.)
After modal verbs (können, müssen ...), however, 'zu' is dropped: Ich kann Deutsch lernen.

rule.en:
Formation
zu + infinitive goes at the end of the sentence, after another verb or fixed expression.

Verbwith zu
lernenzu lernen
einkaufen (separable)einzukaufen
aufhören (separable)aufzuhören

With separable verbs, zu goes between the prefix and the stem: ein-zu-kaufen.

When do we use it?
After certain expressions:
• Es ist wichtig, ... zu ...
• Ich habe Lust, ... zu ...
• Ich versuche/vergesse/plane, ... zu ...

Examples
Ich versuche, Deutsch zu lernen.
Es ist schön, einzukaufen.
Vergiss nicht, die Tür zuzumachen.

Careful: After modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen ...) zu is NOT used: Ich kann Deutsch lernen. (no zu)

explanation.en:
sowohl ... als auch and weder ... noch are two-part connectors that link two similar parts of a sentence.
sowohl ... als auch = Plus + Plus: both things are true.
weder ... noch = Minus + Minus: neither thing is true.
Example: Ich spreche sowohl Englisch als auch Deutsch. (both are true — I speak both English and German.)
Er trinkt weder Kaffee noch Tee. (neither one — He drinks neither coffee nor tea.)
Tip: with weder ... noch the sentence doesn't need an extra 'nicht'.

rule.en:
Structure
ConnectorMeaning
sowohl ... als auchPlus + Plus (both are true)
weder ... nochMinus + Minus (neither is true)

Both are two-part connectors that link two parallel sentence parts (e.g. two nouns, two verbs, two adjectives).

Word order
With weder ... noch, the sentence stays grammatically positive — no extra 'nicht' or 'kein' is needed.

Examples
Ich spreche sowohl Englisch als auch Deutsch.
Er trinkt weder Kaffee noch Tee.
Sie ist weder müde noch hungrig.

explanation.en:
Modal verbs change the meaning of the main verb. müssen = obligation, dürfen = permission (with nicht = prohibition), sollen = task/advice, können = ability, wollen = wish.
Sentence structure: modal verb in position 2, main verb in the infinitive right at the end.
Example: Hier darf man nicht rauchen. (You're not allowed to smoke here.) Du musst leise sein. (You have to be quiet.)
Careful: nicht dürfen (forbidden) is NOT the same as nicht müssen (not necessary)!

rule.en:
Modal verbs — overview
VerbMeaning
müssenobligation, necessity
dürfenpermission; with 'nicht' = prohibition
sollentask or advice (from someone else)
könnenability, possibility
wollenwish, intention
möchtenpolite wish

Sentence structure
Modal verb = position 2 (conjugated), main verb = infinitive at the end.
Hier darf man nicht rauchen.
Du musst leise sein.

Careful: nicht dürfen = prohibition, but nicht müssen = no obligation (not the same thing!).
Du musst das nicht machen. (= it's not necessary)
Du darfst das nicht machen. (= it's forbidden)

explanation.en:
Two-way prepositions (in, an, auf, unter, über, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen) take either the accusative or the dative — depending on the question.
Where to? (movement, goal) -> Accusative.
Where? (fixed location) -> Dative.
Example: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch. (Acc. — Where to? I'm putting the book on the table.) Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. (Dat. — Where? The book is lying on the table.)
Tip: first ask yourself whether something is moving (accusative) or staying still (dative).

rule.en:
Two-way prepositions
in, an, auf, unter, über, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen

QuestionCaseMeaning
Where to?Accusativemovement / direction
Where?Dativefixed location, position

Examples
Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch. (Acc. — Where to?)
Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. (Dat. — Where?)
Ich gehe ins Kino. (in + das = ins)
Ich bin im Kino. (in + dem = im)

Tip: Ask yourself first: is there movement toward a goal (Where to?), or is it just a location (Where?).

explanation.en:
Some verbs always need a reflexive pronoun that points back to the subject — in German these are called reflexive verbs.
The reflexive pronouns in the accusative are: mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich.
Position: the pronoun usually comes right after the conjugated verb.
Example: Ich freue mich auf den Urlaub. (I'm looking forward to the vacation.) Wir treffen uns morgen. (We're meeting tomorrow.)
Tip: for ich, du, wir, ihr the pronoun looks just like the regular personal pronoun (mich, dich, uns, euch) — only for er/sie/es and sie/Sie is it always sich.

rule.en:
Reflexive pronouns in the accusative
PersonPronoun
ichmich
dudich
er/sie/essich
wiruns
ihreuch
sie/Siesich

Position
The reflexive pronoun usually comes right after the conjugated verb.

Examples
Ich freue mich auf den Urlaub.
Wir treffen uns morgen.
Er interessiert sich für Musik.

Common reflexive verbs: sich freuen, sich interessieren, sich treffen, sich fühlen, sich erinnern

explanation.en:
A relative clause gives extra information about a noun. The relative pronoun in the nominative (der, die, das, die) is the subject of this subordinate clause, and the verb moves to the end.
Example: Das ist der Mann, der das Auto repariert. (That's the man who is fixing the car.)
In addition: the connector sondern corrects a negation and means 'but instead' — it only appears after nicht/kein.
Example: Ich kaufe nicht Saft, sondern Milch. (I'm not buying juice, but milk.)

rule.en:
Relative pronoun in the nominative
GenderPronoun
masculineder
femininedie
neuterdas
pluraldie

The relative pronoun is the subject of the subordinate clause, and the verb goes at the end.
Das ist der Mann, der das Auto repariert.

sondern
The connector sondern corrects a preceding negation (nicht ..., sondern ... = 'but instead').
Ich kaufe nicht Saft, sondern Milch.

Careful: sondern is only possible after a negation (nicht/kein); otherwise you use aber.

explanation.en:
When the noun in the relative clause is an accusative object (i.e. it 'receives' the action), only the masculine form of the relative pronoun changes to den.
Feminine (die), neuter (das), and plural (die) stay the same as in the nominative.
Position: as with any subordinate clause, the verb goes right to the end.
Example: Das ist der Film, den ich gestern gesehen habe. (That's the movie I watched yesterday.)
Tip: ask yourself who/what performs the action (nominative) and who/what 'receives' it (accusative).

rule.en:
Relative pronoun in the accusative
GenderNominativeAccusative
masculinederden
femininediedie
neuterdasdas
pluraldiedie

Only the masculine form changes (der -> den) when the relative pronoun is an accusative object.

Das ist der Film, den ich gestern gesehen habe.
Das ist die Frau, die ich gestern getroffen habe.

explanation.en:
In German, you can combine two (or more) nouns into one new, longer word — this is called a compound (Kompositum).
Key rule: the LAST noun determines the article (gender) and the plural of the whole word — no matter what gender the other parts have.
Example: die Tischtennisplatte = der Tisch + das Tennis + die Platte -> the last word is 'die Platte', so the whole word is 'die Tischtennisplatte'.
Tip: read compound words from back to front to understand their meaning.

rule.en:
Compounds: noun + noun
Two (or more) nouns are combined into one new word. The last noun determines the article and plural of the whole word.

Noun 1Noun 2Compound
der Tischdas Tennis + die Plattedie Tischtennisplatte
die Schuleder Hofder Schulhof
der Kaffeedie Tassedie Kaffeetasse

Rule: last noun = article; stress falls on the first part of the word.

explanation.en:
When we're not 100% sure but still want to express an assumption, we use modal verbs in Konjunktiv II.
müsste = almost certain (nearly 100%)
dürfte = probably
könnte = maybe, one possibility among several
Example: Es müsste schon 18 Uhr sein. (It must be 6 pm already — I'm almost sure.)
Important: this form expresses a personal assessment, not a proven fact.

rule.en:
Modal verbs for assumptions (Konjunktiv II)
VerbCertainty
müsstevery certain (almost 100%)
dürfteprobably
könntemaybe possible

Examples
Es müsste schon 18 Uhr sein. (I'm almost sure.)
Sie dürfte schon zu Hause sein. (probably)
Er könnte krank sein. (one of several possibilities)

Tip: This form expresses a subjective assessment, not a fact.

explanation.en:
The genitive shows possession or belonging — it answers the question Wessen? (Whose?).
Article: masculine and neuter nouns take the article des plus an -s or -es ending on the noun itself. Feminine and plural nouns take the article der (no extra ending).
Example: Das Auto des Vaters. (The father's car.) Die Tasche der Frau. (The woman's bag.)
Tip: in everyday speech you'll often hear von + dative instead of the genitive (das Auto von meinem Vater) — but the genitive remains the officially correct form.

rule.en:
Genitive — article
GenderArticleNoun ending
masculinedes+ -s/-es
neuterdes+ -s/-es
feminineder—
pluralder—

Usage
The genitive shows possession or belonging (question: Wessen? — Whose?).

Examples
Das Auto des Vaters.
Die Tasche der Frau.
Der Titel des Buches.

Careful: One-syllable nouns more often take -es (des Mannes), multi-syllable nouns usually just -s (des Vaters).

explanation.en:
The connector obwohl (= 'although/even though') introduces a subordinate clause that expresses a contrast or an unexpected situation.
Word order: as with any subordinate clause, the conjugated verb goes right to the end.
Example: Ich gehe spazieren, obwohl es regnet. (I'm going for a walk, even though it's raining.)
Tip: if the obwohl-clause comes first, the main clause starts directly with the verb: Obwohl es regnet, gehe ich spazieren.

rule.en:
Subordinate clause with obwohl
The connector obwohl introduces a concession (contradiction): something happens even though you'd expect otherwise.

Word order
Main clauseSubordinate clause (obwohl ... verb)
Ich gehe spazieren,obwohl es regnet.

The conjugated verb goes right to the end of the subordinate clause.

Examples
Ich gehe spazieren, obwohl es regnet.
Obwohl er müde war, ist er noch ausgegangen. (subordinate clause first -> main clause starts with the verb)

Compare: obwohl (subordinate clause, verb at the end) vs. trotzdem (main clause, position 1) — same meaning, different structure.

explanation.en:
Connectors link two sentences, but depending on the connector, the word order changes differently.
Subordinate-clause connectors (weil, dass, wenn, obwohl) send the verb to the end of the sentence.
Position-0 connectors (aber, denn, oder, und) don't change the word order at all.
Position-1 connectors (deshalb, trotzdem) take slot 1 themselves, with the verb right after.
Example: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil es regnet. (I'm staying home because it's raining.) Es regnet, aber ich gehe raus. (It's raining, but I'm going out.) Es regnet, deshalb bleibe ich hier. (It's raining, so I'm staying here.)

rule.en:
Connectors — word order
PositionConnectorsEffect
End (subordinate clause)weil, dass, wenn, obwohlverb to the end
Position 0aber, denn, oder, undno change in word order
Position 1deshalb, trotzdemverb comes right after

Examples
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil es regnet. (verb at the end)
Es regnet, aber ich gehe raus. (position 0, normal word order)
Es regnet, deshalb bleibe ich hier. (position 1, verb right after)

explanation.en:
You can combine the stem of a verb (without the -en ending) with a noun to form a new word.
Important: the noun at the end gives the whole word its article.
Example: das Wartezimmer (warten + das Zimmer = a room for waiting). die Waschmaschine (waschen + die Maschine = a machine for washing).
Tip: the first part (the verb stem) explains WHAT the noun is used for.

rule.en:
Compounds: verb + noun
The verb stem (verb without -en) is combined with a noun. The noun at the end determines the article.

Verb+ NounCompound
wartendas Zimmerdas Wartezimmer
waschendie Maschinedie Waschmaschine
schwimmendas Baddas Schwimmbad

Rule: verb stem (without -en) + noun; article = article of the noun at the end.

explanation.en:
The Präteritum is the simple past tense, used mainly in writing (stories, reports, news).
Regular verbs: stem + -te- + ending (ich machte).
Irregular verbs: the stem vowel changes, and you need to memorize the form (ich ging, ich schrieb).
Example: Ich machte gestern meine Hausaufgaben. (I did my homework yesterday.)
Tip: in spoken German, people usually use the Perfekt instead of the Präteritum.

rule.en:
Präteritum — overview
Verb typeFormationExample
regularstem + -te- + endingich machte
irregularstem vowel changesich ging, ich schrieb

Usage
The Präteritum is mostly used in writing (reports, narratives); in spoken German, the Perfekt is preferred.

Examples
Ich machte gestern meine Hausaufgaben.
Er ging nach Hause und schrieb einen Brief.

explanation.en:
Deshalb and deswegen mean 'that's why' and express a logical consequence (reason -> expected result).
Trotzdem means 'nevertheless' and expresses an unexpected consequence (reason -> the opposite of what you'd expect).
Word order: all three words take position 1 themselves, immediately followed by the conjugated verb (inversion).
Example: Es regnet, deshalb bleibe ich hier. (logical consequence — It's raining, so I'm staying here.) Es regnet, trotzdem gehe ich raus. (unexpected — It's raining, but I'm going out anyway.)

rule.en:
deshalb / deswegen / trotzdem
WordMeaning
deshalb, deswegenlogical consequence (reason -> result)
trotzdemunexpected consequence (opposing reason -> state)

All three take position 1, immediately followed by the conjugated verb.

Examples
Es regnet, deshalb bleibe ich hier.
Es regnet, trotzdem gehe ich raus.

explanation.en:
When you combine two nouns into a compound, it often sounds better with a small linking element (Fugenelement) in between — usually -s-, -n-, or -e-.
Example: die Arbeit + der Geber = der Arbeitsgeber. die Frage + der Bogen = der Fragenbogen.
Important: there's no fixed rule for which element to use — it's best to simply memorize new compounds together with their linking element.

rule.en:
Linking elements (Fugenelemente)
Sometimes a compound needs a linking element between the nouns.

ElementExample
-s-die Arbeit + der Geber = der Arbeitsgeber
-n-die Frage + der Bogen = der Fragenbogen
-e-der Hund + die Hütte = die Hundehütte

Tip: There's no fixed rule — it's best to simply learn new compounds together with their linking element.

explanation.en:
The genitive sounds formal and is often used in written language. In everyday spoken German, it's usually replaced by von + dative — which is simpler.
Example: Das Auto des Bruders (genitive, formal) -> Das Auto von meinem Bruder (von + dative, everyday).
Tip: with proper names, von is even required: die Tasche von Anna (not 'Annas Tasche' in spoken language).

rule.en:
Genitive vs. von + Dative
Genitive (formal)von + Dative (everyday)
das Auto des Brudersdas Auto von meinem Bruder

In everyday and spoken language, the genitive is often replaced by von + dative.

Examples
Das Auto des Bruders. (formal, genitive)
Das Auto von meinem Bruder. (everyday, von + dative)

Tip: With names and certain constructions, von is even required: die Freundin von Tom.

explanation.en:
The connectors seit and seitdem (= 'since') show: an action started in the past and is still continuing today.
Position: as in any subordinate clause, the conjugated verb goes right to the end.
Example: Seitdem ich in Deutschland wohne, lerne ich täglich Deutsch. (Since I've been living in Germany, I've been learning German every day.)
Important: even though the action started in the past, the present tense is usually used — because it's still ongoing!

rule.en:
Subordinate clause with seit / seitdem
The connectors seit and seitdem show: an action began in the past and continues up to now.

ConnectorExample
seit / seitdemSeitdem ich in Deutschland wohne, lerne ich täglich Deutsch.

As with all subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb goes at the end.

Careful: The present tense is usually used, even though the action began in the past (because it's still ongoing).

title.en: Verbs with prepositions: questions about people and things

explanation.en:
Some verbs have a fixed preposition (e.g. warten auf). Which question form you use depends on whether it's about a person or a thing.
People: preposition + wen/wem — Auf wen wartest du? (Who are you waiting for?)
Things: Wo(r) + preposition — Worauf wartest du? (What are you waiting for?)
Example: Auf wen wartest du? – Auf meinen Freund. (person) Worauf wartest du? – Auf den Bus. (thing)

rule.en:
Questions about people and things
PeopleThings
Questionpreposition + wen/wemwo(r) + preposition
ExampleAuf wen wartest du?Worauf wartest du?

Rule for things: if the preposition starts with a vowel, an -r- is inserted: worauf, worüber, woran.

Examples
Auf wen wartest du? – Ich warte auf meinen Freund. (person)
Worauf wartest du? – Ich warte auf den Bus. (thing)

explanation.en:
The connector bis shows the endpoint of an action or period of time — 'until when?'.
It introduces a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes right to the end of the sentence.
Example: Ich warte hier, bis du kommst. (I'll wait here until you come.)
Tip: don't confuse the connector bis with the preposition bis + noun (bis Montag — until Monday) — here a full clause with its own subject and verb follows.

rule.en:
Subordinate clause with bis
The connector bis shows the endpoint of an action or time period (until when?). It's a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes at the end.

Main clauseSubordinate clause (bis ... verb)
Ich warte hier,bis du kommst.

Examples
Ich warte hier, bis du kommst.
Wir bleiben, bis der Film zu Ende ist.

Compare with the preposition: bis + noun (bis Montag) vs. bis + subordinate clause (bis du kommst).

explanation.en:
Almost any verb can be turned into a noun — this is called a nominalized infinitive.
Rule: just capitalize the infinitive; the noun always takes the article das and usually has no plural.
Example: leben -> das Leben (life), essen -> das Essen (food), lernen -> das Lernen (learning).
This form is often used to talk about an activity in general: Das Lernen einer Sprache braucht Zeit. (Learning a language takes time.)

rule.en:
Nominalized infinitive
Almost any verb can become a noun: simply capitalize the infinitive. The noun is always neuter (article das).

VerbNoun
lebendas Leben
essendas Essen
lernendas Lernen

Examples
Das Lernen einer Sprache braucht Zeit.
Das Essen schmeckt gut.

Tip: These nouns normally have no plural.

explanation.en:
When we talk about things (not people!), we use special words instead of preposition + 'it'.
For questions: wo- + preposition (e.g. worüber = 'about what?').
For answers/references: da- + preposition (e.g. darüber = 'about it/that').
If the preposition starts with a vowel, an -r- is inserted: worüber, darüber.
Example: Worüber sprecht ihr? (What are you talking about?) Wir sprechen darüber. (We're talking about it.)
Careful: for people, you instead say preposition + wen/wem: Über wen sprecht ihr? (Who are you talking about?)

rule.en:
Prepositional adverbs: wo- / da-
FunctionFormExample
Question (thing)wo(r)- + prepositionWorüber sprecht ihr?
Answer / reference (thing)da(r)- + prepositionWir sprechen darüber.

If the preposition starts with a vowel, an -r- is inserted: worüber, darüber, woran, daran.

Careful: For people, we do NOT use prepositional adverbs — instead: preposition + wen/wem: Über wen sprecht ihr? — Über ihn.

explanation.en:
Futur I describes plans, promises, or predictions about the future.
Formation: werden (conjugated, position 2) + infinitive of the main verb (end of sentence).
Example: Ich werde morgen das Auto waschen. (I will wash the car tomorrow.)
Tip: in everyday speech, people often just use the present tense + a time expression (Ich wasche morgen das Auto) — Futur I sounds more formal and especially emphasizes a promise or a prediction.

rule.en:
Futur I: werden + infinitive
Personwerden
ichwerde
duwirst
er/sie/eswird
wirwerden
ihrwerdet
sie/Siewerden

Sentence structure
werden (position 2) + ... + infinitive (end of sentence).
Ich werde morgen das Auto waschen.

Usage
Plans, promises, predictions about the future.

Tip: In everyday speech, people often just use the present tense + a time expression (Ich wasche morgen das Auto). Futur I especially emphasizes a promise or a prediction.

explanation.en:
The two-part connector nicht nur ..., sondern auch ... ('not only..., but also...') links two statements and emphasizes that BOTH are true at the same time — often the second point is surprising or especially important.
Example: Er ist nicht nur intelligent, sondern auch sehr sportlich. (He's not only smart, but also very athletic.)
Compare: similar to sowohl ... als auch, but with stronger emphasis on the second part.

rule.en:
nicht nur ..., sondern auch ...
A two-part connector that links two positive aspects, emphasizing that both apply at the same time.

Part 1Part 2
nicht nursondern auch

Examples
Er ist nicht nur intelligent, sondern auch sehr sportlich.
Sie spricht nicht nur Deutsch, sondern auch Französisch.

Tip: Similar to sowohl ... als auch, but with a stronger emphasis on the second (often surprising) part.

title.en: Clauses with um … zu (in order to)

explanation.en:
With um ... zu + infinitive, we express an intention or a goal (question: What for?).
Key condition: this only works when the subject in the main clause and the subordinate clause is exactly the same.
Example: Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Deutschland zu arbeiten. (I learn = I work, same subject — I'm learning German in order to work in Germany.)
Tip: if the subject is different, you need damit + its own verb instead.

rule.en:
Sentences with um ... zu
This construction expresses a goal or intention (question: Wozu? — What for?).

ConditionConstruction
same subjectum ... zu + infinitive
different subjectdamit + subordinate clause

Examples
Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Deutschland zu arbeiten. (subject ich = ich)

Careful: um ... zu only works when the subject is the same in both parts of the sentence. Otherwise you need damit.

explanation.en:
When the subject in the main clause and the subordinate clause is DIFFERENT, we MUST use damit instead of um ... zu.
Word order: as in any subordinate clause, the conjugated verb goes right to the end.
Example: Ich gebe meinem Sohn Geld, damit er ein Buch kauft. (Subject 1: I; subject 2: he — different!)
Compare: Ich lerne, um die Prüfung zu bestehen. (same subject) vs. Der Lehrer erklärt es langsam, damit wir es verstehen. (different subject)

rule.en:
Review: subordinate clause with damit
ConditionConstruction
same subjectum ... zu
different subjectdamit + subordinate clause

With damit, the conjugated verb goes to the end of the subordinate clause.

Examples
Ich gebe meinem Sohn Geld, damit er ein Buch kauft. (subject 1: ich; subject 2: er — different, so damit)

Compare: Ich lerne, um die Prüfung zu bestehen. (same subject) vs. Der Lehrer erklärt es langsam, damit wir es verstehen. (different subjects)

explanation.en:
From many adjectives you can form a noun with the suffixes -heit or -keit, describing a quality or characteristic.
Important: these nouns are ALWAYS feminine — article die, no exceptions.
Example: krank -> die Krankheit (illness), einsam -> die Einsamkeit (loneliness).
Tip: -keit usually follows adjectives ending in -ig, -lich, -bar (möglich -> Möglichkeit), otherwise it's usually -heit.

rule.en:
Word formation: nouns ending in -heit / -keit
AdjectiveNoun
krankdie Krankheit
freidie Freiheit
einsamdie Einsamkeit
möglichdie Möglichkeit

Rule: These nouns are ALWAYS feminine (article die).

Tip: -keit usually follows adjectives ending in -ig, -lich, -bar (möglich -> Möglichkeit), otherwise it's usually -heit.

explanation.en:
In the passive voice, the action itself is the focus, not the person performing it — often because that person is unknown or unimportant.
Formation: werden (conjugated, position 2) + Partizip II (end of sentence).
Example: Der Mechaniker repariert das Auto. (Active — The mechanic repairs the car.) -> Das Auto wird repariert. (Passive, without saying who — The car is being repaired.)
Tip: ask yourself: does it matter WHO performs the action? If not, use the passive.

rule.en:
Passive voice (present tense)
ActivePassive
Der Mechaniker repariert das Auto.Das Auto wird repariert.

Formation
werden (conjugated, position 2) + Partizip II (end of sentence).

Personwerden
ichwerde
duwirst
er/sie/eswird
wirwerden
ihrwerdet
sie/Siewerden

Examples
Das Auto wird repariert.
Die Fenster werden geputzt.

Tip: The passive is used when it's not important or not known who performs the action.

explanation.en:
The Perfekt is the most common past tense in spoken German.
Formation: haben or sein (conjugated, position 2) + Partizip II (end of sentence).
When sein, when haben? sein for movement (gehen, laufen) or change of state (aufwachen) — otherwise always haben.
Example: Ich habe geschlafen. (I slept.) Er ist gekommen. (He came.)
Tip: when in doubt: most verbs take haben, only a smaller group needs sein.

rule.en:
Review: Perfekt
Auxiliary verbWhen?
seinmovement (gehen, fahren) or change of state (aufwachen, einschlafen)
habenall other verbs (default case)

Formation
haben/sein (position 2) + Partizip II (end of sentence).

Examples
Ich habe geschlafen.
Er ist gekommen.
Wir sind nach Berlin gefahren.

Tip: In spoken German, the Perfekt is the most commonly used past tense.

explanation.en:
You can form a noun from many verbs by replacing the -en ending with the suffix -ung.
Important: these nouns are ALWAYS feminine (article die) and usually describe a process or result.
Example: wohnen -> die Wohnung (apartment), einladen -> die Einladung (invitation), lösen -> die Lösung (solution).
Tip: this ending is very productive — many new nouns in German are formed exactly this way.

rule.en:
Word formation: nouns ending in -ung
VerbNoun
wohnendie Wohnung
einladendie Einladung
lösendie Lösung

Rule: verb without -en + suffix -ung. These nouns are ALWAYS feminine (article die) and usually describe a process or a result.

Examples
Die Wohnung ist groß.
Danke für die Einladung.

explanation.en:
Many verbs are permanently linked to a certain preposition, and that preposition determines the case — you have to learn both together.
Important for B1: sich interessieren für (+ accusative), träumen von (+ dative), sich freuen auf (+ accusative, for the future), sich freuen über (+ accusative, for the present).
Example: Ich interessiere mich für Musik. (I'm interested in music.) Wir freuen uns auf den Urlaub. (still to come — We're looking forward to the vacation.)
Tip: always learn verb + preposition as one fixed pair, not separately.

rule.en:
Verbs with prepositions — review
VerbPrepositionCase
sich interessieren fürfürAccusative
träumen vonvonDative
sich freuen aufaufAccusative (future)
sich freuen überüberAccusative (present)

Examples
Ich interessiere mich für Musik.
Sie träumt von einer Reise.
Wir freuen uns auf den Urlaub. (something still to come)
Wir freuen uns über das Geschenk. (already happened)

title.en: Question words with wo(r)- and prepositional adverbs with da(r)-

explanation.en:
When we ask or answer about things (not people), we replace preposition + 'it' with special words using wo- or da-.
Question: wo(r)- + preposition (e.g. wovon).
Answer/reference: da(r)- + preposition (e.g. davon).
Example: Wovon träumst du? (What are you dreaming of?) Ich träume davon. (I'm dreaming of it.)
Careful: for people we instead ask with preposition + wen/wem: Von wem träumst du?

rule.en:
Question words with wo(r)- and da(r)-
FunctionFormExample
Question (thing)wo(r)- + prepositionWovon träumst du?
Answer / reference (thing)da(r)- + prepositionIch träume davon.

Before a vowel, an -r- is inserted: worauf, darauf, worüber, darüber.

Careful: For people, we ask with preposition + wen/wem: Von wem träumst du? — Von ihr.

title.en: Showing interest with denn and eigentlich

explanation.en:
Denn and eigentlich are modal particles — small words with no fixed translation that make questions sound friendlier and more natural.
denn shows genuine interest in the answer. eigentlich shows casual curiosity or introduces a change of topic.
Example: Wie heißt du denn? (So what's your name?) Woher kommst du eigentlich? (So where are you actually from?)
Tip: these words go after the subject or verb, never at the start of the sentence.

rule.en:
Modal particles: denn and eigentlich
ParticleFunction
dennshows genuine interest, makes questions friendlier
eigentlichintroduces a change of topic or shows casual curiosity

These words don't change the meaning of the sentence — they just make it sound more natural in conversation.

Examples
Wie heißt du denn?
Woher kommst du eigentlich?

Tip: Modal particles usually go right after the subject or verb, never at the start of the sentence.

explanation.en:
The prefix un- before an adjective flips its meaning to the opposite — it's a kind of negation built right into the word.
Example: glücklich -> unglücklich (unhappy), freundlich -> unfreundlich (unfriendly), wichtig -> unwichtig (unimportant).
Stress: un- is pronounced with stress.
Careful: not every adjective works this way — some have their own separate opposite word (gut -> schlecht, NOT *ungut).

rule.en:
Word formation: adjectives with un-
AdjectiveOpposite
glücklichunglücklich
freundlichunfreundlich
wichtigunwichtig

Rule: un- + adjective = opposite (negation). The stress falls on un-.

Examples
Er war den ganzen Tag unglücklich.
Sie war sehr unfreundlich zu mir.
Das ist doch total unwichtig!

Careful: Not every adjective forms its opposite with un- — some have their own separate word (gut -> schlecht, not *ungut).

explanation.en:
To express a (often unrealistic) wish, we use Konjunktiv II: wäre (sein), hätte (haben), or würde + infinitive (other verbs).
These sentences are often reinforced with doch or nur.
Example: Ich wäre gern am Strand! (I wish I were at the beach!) Wenn ich nur mehr Zeit hätte! (If only I had more time!)
Tip: this form shows that the wish is not (yet) reality.

rule.en:
Konjunktiv II: expressing wishes
VerbKonjunktiv II
seinwäre
habenhätte
other verbswürde + infinitive

Structure for wishes
Often reinforced with doch, nur, or doch nur.

Examples
Ich wäre gern am Strand! (I wish I were at the beach!)
Wenn ich nur mehr Zeit hätte! (If only I had more time!)
Ich würde gern mehr reisen. (I'd love to travel more.)

Tip: These sentences express a wish that isn't (yet) reality.

title.en: Subordinate clause with wenn in Subjunctive II (unreal conditions)

explanation.en:
When we talk about a condition that isn't real (or is very unlikely), we use wenn + Konjunktiv II in BOTH parts of the sentence.
Structure: wenn-clause (verb at the end) + main clause with würde + infinitive (or its own Konjunktiv II).
Example: Wenn ich viel Geld hätte, würde ich ein Haus kaufen. (If I had a lot of money, I would buy a house.)
Tip: you can also reverse the order: Ich würde ein Haus kaufen, wenn ich viel Geld hätte.

rule.en:
Unreal conditional sentences with wenn + Konjunktiv II
PartForm
wenn-clause (condition)wenn ... Konjunktiv II ... verb at the end
main clause (result)würde + infinitive (or Konjunktiv II)

Example
Wenn ich viel Geld hätte, würde ich ein Haus kaufen.

Usage
The condition is unrealistic or unlikely (contrary to reality).

Tip: You can also put the main clause first: Ich würde ein Haus kaufen, wenn ich viel Geld hätte.

explanation.en:
When a whole subordinate clause (instead of a simple noun) follows a verb with a fixed preposition, we need a bridge: a prepositional adverb (darauf, darüber...) + dass.
Example: Ich freue mich auf den Besuch. (noun) -> Ich freue mich darauf, dass du mich besuchst. (subordinate clause)
Tip: the prepositional adverb goes in the main clause, and dass + verb-at-the-end goes in the subordinate clause.

rule.en:
Verbs with preposition + dass-clause
When a whole clause (subordinate clause) follows a prepositional verb, we use a prepositional adverb (da(r)-) + dass.

StructureExample
verb + prepositional adverb + dass + subordinate clauseIch freue mich darauf, dass du mich besuchst.

More examples
Ich ärgere mich darüber, dass es regnet.
Sie hofft darauf, dass alles gut geht.

Careful: Without this construction, with a noun: Ich freue mich auf den Besuch. With a subordinate clause: Ich freue mich darauf, dass du kommst.

title.en: Word formation: adjectives ending in -ig/-isch before nouns

explanation.en:
You can form adjectives from nouns by adding -ig or -isch.
Example: der Wind -> windig (windy), die Sonne -> sonnig (sunny), die Romantik -> romantisch (romantic).
Important: when these adjectives come before a noun, they must be declined normally — just like any other adjective.
Example: ein windiger Tag (a windy day), ein romantisches Buch (a romantic book).
Tip: -isch often appears with countries and languages (Deutschland -> deutsch).

rule.en:
Word formation: adjectives ending in -ig / -isch
NounAdjective
der Windwindig
die Sonnesonnig
die Romantikromantisch

Declining before a noun
These adjectives decline just like any other.
ein windiger Tag (masculine, Nom.)
ein romantisches Buch (neuter, Nom.)

Tip: -isch often appears with countries, languages, or abstract concepts (typisch, chemisch, historisch).

explanation.en:
The connector bevor (= 'before') puts two actions in time order: the action in the main clause happens FIRST, the one in the bevor-clause happens AFTER.
Position: as in any subordinate clause, the conjugated verb goes right to the end.
Example: Wasch deine Hände, bevor du isst. (Wash your hands before you eat.)
Tip: the opposite is nachdem — it reverses the order (the subordinate-clause action happens first).

rule.en:
Subordinate clause with bevor
The connector bevor shows: the action in the main clause happens first, the one in the subordinate clause happens afterward.

OrderSentence part
1. firstmain clause
2. thenbevor-clause

As always, the conjugated verb goes at the end of the subordinate clause.

Examples
Wasch deine Hände, bevor du isst.
Bevor ich ins Bett gehe, putze ich mir die Zähne. (subordinate clause first -> main clause starts with the verb)

Opposite: nachdem — reverses the order (the subordinate-clause action happens first).

title.en: Adjective endings after the definite and indefinite article

explanation.en:
After the definite article (der/die/das), the adjective usually gets a weak ending: -e in the nominative, otherwise usually -en — because the article itself already shows gender and case.
After the indefinite article (ein/eine), this signal is sometimes missing, so in the nominative/accusative the adjective takes over the ending: -er, -es, -e.
Example: der neue Lehrer (definite) vs. ein neuer Lehrer (indefinite).
Tip: ask yourself first: does the article already show gender/case? If not, the adjective has to do it.

rule.en:
Adjective declension — overview
Caseafter definite articleafter indefinite article
Nom. masc.-e (der gute Mann)-er (ein guter Mann)
Nom./Acc. neut.-e (das gute Kind)-es (ein gutes Kind)
Nom./Acc. fem.-e (die gute Frau)-e (eine gute Frau)
all other cases-en-en

Rule
After the definite article, the article itself usually already carries the information (gender/case) — the adjective gets the weak ending -e or -en.
After the indefinite article, the adjective itself shows the missing signal in the nominative and accusative (masc./neut.): -er, -es, -e.

Examples
Der neue Lehrer ist nett. (definite)
Ein neuer Lehrer ist da. (indefinite, masc., Nom.)

explanation.en:
When a comparative form (kleiner) or superlative form (kleinste) comes directly before a noun, it ALSO gets the regular adjective ending.
Example: ein kleineres Auto (comparative kleiner + ending -es). das kleinste Haus (superlative kleinst + ending -e).
Tip: think in two steps: first form the comparative/superlative, then add the matching ending just like for any adjective.

rule.en:
Comparative / superlative before a noun
FormExample
Comparative + adjective endingein kleineres Auto
Superlative + adjective endingdas kleinste Haus

Formation
Comparative: adjective + -er + regular ending.
Superlative: adjective + -st (or -est) + regular ending.

Examples
ein kleineres Auto (comparative + -es, neuter, indefinite article)
das kleinste Haus (superlative + -e, neuter, definite article)
die schnellsten Autos (superlative, plural)

title.en: Word formation: adjectives used as nouns

explanation.en:
Some adjectives can become nouns — they're capitalized but keep their adjective endings when declined (they don't behave like regular nouns!).
Example: bekannt -> der Bekannte / ein Bekannter (acquaintance). neu -> etwas Neues (something new).
Tip: gender depends on the person: der Bekannte (man), die Bekannte (woman) — the ending follows the normal adjective rules.

rule.en:
Word formation: adjectives as nouns
AdjectiveNoun
bekanntder Bekannte / ein Bekannter
neuetwas Neues
krankder/die Kranke

Rule
These nouns are capitalized but keep their adjective endings — they decline just like ordinary adjectives!

Examples
Ich habe einen Bekannten getroffen.
Gibt es etwas Neues?

Tip: Gender depends on the person: der Bekannte (masc.), die Bekannte (fem.).

explanation.en:
nicht brauchen zu + infinitive means exactly the same as nicht müssen — namely: it's NOT necessary, no obligation.
Example: Du brauchst heute nicht zu arbeiten. (= You don't have to work today.)
Tip: this form sounds a bit more formal and is often combined with nur: Du brauchst nur anzurufen. (You just need to call.)

rule.en:
nicht brauchen zu
ConstructionMeaning
nicht müssenno obligation
nicht brauchen zu + infinitiveno obligation (same meaning)

Examples
Du brauchst heute nicht zu arbeiten. (= Du musst nicht arbeiten.)
Sie braucht das nicht zu erklären.

Tip: This form is a bit more formal and is often combined with nur: Du brauchst nur anzurufen. (You just need to call.)

explanation.en:
The connector während links two actions that happen exactly at the same time (simultaneously).
Position: it's a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes at the end.
Example: Während ich koche, hört mein Mann Musik. (While I'm cooking, my husband is listening to music.)
Second meaning: während can also express a contrast (= 'whereas'): Er ist faul, während sie sehr fleißig ist. (He's lazy, whereas she's very hard-working.)

rule.en:
Subordinate clause with während
The connector während shows: two actions happen at the same time (simultaneously).

Subordinate clauseMain clause
Während ich koche,hört mein Mann Musik.

As always, the conjugated verb goes at the end of the subordinate clause.

Examples
Während ich koche, hört mein Mann Musik.
Mein Mann hört Musik, während ich koche. (main clause first)

Second meaning: während can also express a contrast (whereas): Er ist faul, während sie sehr fleißig ist.

explanation.en:
Indefinite pronouns (jemand, niemand, etwas, alles) refer to an unspecified person or thing — you don't know exactly who or what is meant.
Possessive pronouns in the absolute form (meins, deins, seins, ihrs) can replace a whole noun once it's already clear from context.
Example: Jemand hat angerufen. (Someone called.) Ist das dein Stift? Nein, das ist meins. (Is that your pen? No, that's mine.)
Tip: the possessive pronoun without a noun behind it agrees in gender and case with the noun it replaces.

rule.en:
Indefinite pronouns and possessive pronouns
TypeExamples
Indefinite pronounsjemand, niemand, etwas, alles
Possessive pronouns (absolute form)meins, deins, seins, ihrs

Indefinite pronouns replace an unspecified person or thing. Possessive pronouns in this form replace a whole noun once it's already known.

Examples
Jemand hat angerufen. (Someone called.)
Ich habe nichts gehört. (I heard nothing.)
Ist das dein Stift? Nein, das ist meins. (Is that your pen? No, that's mine.)

explanation.en:
The suffix -chen turns a noun into a smaller or cuter version of itself (diminutive).
Important: such words are ALWAYS neuter (article das) — even if the original noun had a different gender!
Example: das Brot -> das Brötchen, die Katze -> das Kätzchen (die -> das!).
Tip: the stem vowel often gets an umlaut (a->ä, o->ö, u->ü): Haus -> Häuschen.

rule.en:
Word formation: nouns ending in -chen
NounDiminutive
das Brotdas Brötchen
die Katzedas Kätzchen
das Hausdas Häuschen

Rule: All nouns ending in -chen are ALWAYS neuter (das), even if the original word had a different gender. The stem vowel often gets an umlaut (a->ä, o->ö, u->ü).

Examples
Das Brötchen schmeckt frisch.
Was für ein süßes Kätzchen!

explanation.en:
The Plusquamperfekt (past perfect) describes an action that happened even BEFORE another action in the past — the 'past of the past'.
Formation: Präteritum of haben/sein (hatte/war) + Partizip II at the end.
Example: Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, ging ich schlafen. (first: ate, then: went to sleep)
Tip: this tense almost always appears together with nachdem.

rule.en:
Plusquamperfekt (past perfect)
Time levelExample
1. first (Plusquamperfekt)Ich hatte gegessen.
2. then (Präteritum)Ich ging schlafen.

Formation
Präteritum of haben or sein (hatte / war) + Partizip II at the end.

Examples
Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, ging ich schlafen.
Sie war schon gegangen, als ich ankam.

Usage: Only for an even earlier past — usually combined with nachdem.

explanation.en:
An infinitive can be used directly as a noun to describe an activity in general.
Rule: capitalized, ALWAYS with the article das (because it comes from the verb, unlike a regular noun).
Example: rauchen -> Das Rauchen ist hier verboten. (Smoking is forbidden here.) lesen -> Das Lesen macht Spaß. (Reading is fun.)
Tip: this form is a compact alternative to 'Es ist verboten zu rauchen'.

rule.en:
Infinitive as a noun
InfinitiveNoun
rauchendas Rauchen
lesendas Lesen

Rule: The infinitive is capitalized and always takes the article das. It describes a general activity or process.

Examples
Das Rauchen ist hier verboten.
Das Lesen macht Spaß.

Tip: This construction is an alternative to verbs with zu: Rauchen verboten! = Es ist verboten zu rauchen.

explanation.en:
The connector nachdem shows that the action in the subordinate clause happened BEFORE the action in the main clause.
Key tense rule: if the main clause is in the Präteritum, the nachdem-clause MUST be in the Plusquamperfekt. If the main clause is in the present tense, the nachdem-clause uses the Perfekt.
Example: Nachdem er die Hausaufgabe gemacht hatte, spielte er Fußball. (Plusquamperfekt -> Präteritum)
Tip: with nachdem, getting the tense right is especially important — unlike with most subordinate clauses!

rule.en:
Subordinate clause with nachdem
Main-clause tensenachdem-clause tense
PräsensPerfekt
PräteritumPlusquamperfekt

Rule: The action in the nachdem-clause happens BEFORE the action in the main clause — that's why it's in an earlier time level.

Examples
Nachdem er die Hausaufgabe gemacht hatte, spielte er Fußball. (Plusquamperfekt -> Präteritum)
Nachdem ich gegessen habe, gehe ich spazieren. (Perfekt -> Präsens)

Careful: Unlike most subordinate clauses, with nachdem the tense really matters!

explanation.en:
With the suffixes -bar and -los, you can form a new adjective from a verb or a noun.
-bar (usually from verbs) means 'this can be done' (= possible).
-los (usually from nouns) means 'without something' (= missing).
Example: essen -> essbar (edible, can be eaten). das Geld -> geldlos (without money). die Arbeit -> arbeitslos (unemployed).
Tip: ask yourself: does the word come from a verb (-bar) or a noun (-los)?

rule.en:
Word formation: adjectives ending in -bar and -los
SuffixMeaningExample
-barcan be done (possible)essen -> essbar
-loswithout something (missing)das Geld -> geldlos

Examples
Dieser Pilz ist nicht essbar. (This mushroom isn't edible.)
Er ist seit einem Jahr arbeitslos. (He's been unemployed for a year.)

Tip: -bar almost always comes from verbs (lesen -> lesbar), -los almost always from nouns (die Hoffnung -> hoffnungslos).

explanation.en:
You can also combine the passive with a modal verb to say that something MUST, CAN, or SHOULD be done.
Structure: modal verb (conjugated, position 2) + ... + Partizip II + werden (infinitive, right at the end).
Example: Das Haus muss renoviert werden. (= Someone has to renovate the house, but we don't say who — The house needs to be renovated.)
Tip: so at the end of the sentence there are TWO words: first the Partizip II, then werden.

rule.en:
Passive with modal verbs
Position 2End of sentence
modal verb (conjugated)Partizip II + werden (infinitive)

Examples
Das Haus muss renoviert werden. (The house must be renovated.)
Die Aufgabe kann heute nicht gemacht werden. (The task can't be done today.)

Compare
Active: Man muss das Haus renovieren.
Passive: Das Haus muss renoviert werden.

explanation.en:
The prepositions während (duration), wegen (reason), and trotz (despite) always require the genitive in official/written German.
Example: Wegen des Regens bleiben wir hier. (Because of the rain, we're staying here.) Trotz der Kälte geht er raus. (Despite the cold, he's going out.)
Tip: in spoken language you'll often hear wegen + dative (wegen dem Regen), but the genitive remains officially correct.

rule.en:
Prepositions with the genitive
PrepositionMeaning
währendduration
wegenreason
trotzdespite

Examples
Wegen des Regens bleiben wir hier. (Because of the rain, we're staying here.)
Trotz der Kälte geht er raus. (Despite the cold, he's going out.)
Während der Ferien arbeite ich nicht. (During the holidays I don't work.)

Tip: In spoken language, people often use wegen + dative instead of the genitive (wegen dem Regen) — but the genitive remains the officially correct form.

title.en: Adjective ending in the genitive case

explanation.en:
In the genitive, the adjective ending is especially simple: after the definite OR indefinite article, ALL adjectives (no matter the gender) take the ending -en.
Example: wegen des schlechten Wetters (because of the bad weather), trotz einer großen Pause (despite a long break).
Tip: this is the only case in German with no exceptions — in the genitive you only need to remember ONE ending!

rule.en:
Adjective ending in the genitive
Gender / numberEnding
masculine-en
neuter-en
feminine-en
plural-en

Rule: In the genitive, EVERY adjective (after a definite or indefinite article) takes the ending -en — no matter the gender.

Examples
wegen des schlechten Wetters. (because of the bad weather)
trotz einer großen Pause. (despite a long break)

Tip: This makes the genitive simpler than the other cases — there are no exceptions to learn!

explanation.en:
You can form an adjective from a noun by adding -voll or -reich — both mean 'a lot of this noun'.
-voll tends to emphasize a quality, -reich tends to emphasize an amount or abundance.
Example: der Humor -> humorvoll (very funny, full of humor). das Vitamin -> vitaminreich (full of vitamins).
Tip: both suffixes are productive — you can attach them to many nouns.

rule.en:
Word formation: adjectives ending in -voll and -reich
NounAdjective
der Humorhumorvoll
das Vitaminvitaminreich

Rule: Both suffixes mean 'a lot of this noun'. -voll tends to emphasize a quality, -reich tends to emphasize an amount or abundance.

Examples
Ein humorvoller Freund. (A friend with a great sense of humor.)
Ein vitaminreiches Frühstück. (A vitamin-rich breakfast.)

explanation.en:
Some masculine nouns (often people or professions ending in -e, -ent, -ist, -at) get an extra -n or -en in ALL cases except the nominative — this is called the n-declension.
Example: der Kollege (Nom.) -> Ich helfe dem Kollegen (Dat. — I'm helping my colleague). Ich sehe den Kollegen (Acc. — I see my colleague).
Tip: only the nominative stays normal — it's best to memorize these nouns as their own group.

rule.en:
n-declension (n-Deklination)
CaseForm
Nominativeder Kollege
Accusativeden Kollegen
Dativedem Kollegen
Genitivedes Kollegen

Rule: Certain masculine nouns (often people, ending in -e, -ent, -ist, -at) get an extra -n or -en in ALL cases except the nominative.

Examples
Ich helfe dem Kollegen. (Dative)
Ich sehe den Kollegen. (Accusative)

More examples: der Student -> den/dem/des Studenten; der Junge -> den/dem/des Jungen.

explanation.en:
Review and expansion: If the noun requires a dative object in the relative clause, we use the pronouns dem (masc. / neutr.), der (fem.), and denen (watch out for plural!).
Example: Das sind die Freunde, denen ich helfe.

rule.en:
Relative pronoun in the dative
GenderPronoun
masculinedem
feminineder
neuterdem
pluraldenen

Careful: In the plural, the form is denen (with an extra -en), not simply 'den'.

Examples
Das ist die Frau, der ich helfe. (feminine, dative)
Das sind die Freunde, denen ich helfe. (plural, dative)

Tip: The case of the relative pronoun depends on the verb in the subordinate clause (helfen requires the dative).

explanation.en:
If the verb in the relative clause requires a preposition, this preposition is placed directly BEFORE the relative pronoun. The case depends on that preposition.
Example: Das ist die Frau, mit der ich spreche (mit + Dativ fem.).

rule.en:
Relative clause with a preposition
StructureExample
preposition + relative pronoundie Frau, mit der ich spreche

Rule: The preposition determines the case of the relative pronoun (not the verb alone).

Examples
Das ist die Frau, mit der ich spreche. (mit + dative)
Das ist das Buch, über das wir sprechen. (über + accusative)
Das ist der Freund, auf den ich warte. (auf + accusative)

Tip: The preposition and the relative pronoun always stay together at the start of the subordinate clause.

title.en: Relative clause with wo and was

explanation.en:
We use wo as a relative pronoun after city names or locations. We use was after indefinite pronouns like 'alles, etwas, nichts' or abstract superlatives (das Beste).
Example: Das ist alles, was ich weiß.

rule.en:
Relative clause with wo and was
WordWhen?
woafter place or country names, local nouns
wasafter 'alles, etwas, nichts' or superlatives

Examples
Berlin ist eine Stadt, wo man viel erleben kann. (Berlin is a city where you can experience a lot.)
Das ist alles, was ich weiß. (That's all I know.)
Das war das Beste, was mir passieren konnte. (That was the best thing that could have happened to me.)

Tip: wo can be used instead of 'in dem/in der' when talking about a place.

explanation.en:
Prefixes for intensification: Placing super-, hoch-, über-, or extra- in front of an adjective amplifies its meaning to 'very' or 'extremely'.
Example: modern -> supermodern, wichtig -> hochwichtig.

rule.en:
Word formation: adjectives with super-, hoch-, über- and extra-
PrefixExample
super-modern -> supermodern
hoch-wichtig -> hochwichtig
über-empfindlich -> überempfindlich
extra-stark -> extrastark

Rule: These prefixes intensify the meaning of the adjective (= 'very' or 'extremely'). The stress usually falls on the prefix.

Examples
Das Handy ist supermodern. (The phone is super modern.)
Das Thema ist hochwichtig. (The topic is extremely important.)

explanation.en:
If there is no article before the noun (null article), the adjective itself MUST carry the grammatical ending. Masculine Nom. -> -er, neutral Nom. -> -es, feminine Nom. -> -e.
Example: Kalter Kaffee schmeckt nicht.

rule.en:
Adjective declension without an article
Casemasculineneuterfeminineplural
Nominative-er-es-e-e
Dative-em-em-er-en

Rule: Without an article (zero article), the adjective itself must show the gender and case of the noun — just like the definite article normally would.

Examples
Kalter Kaffee schmeckt nicht. (masculine, Nom. — Cold coffee doesn't taste good.)
Ich trinke Tee mit warmer Milch. (feminine, Dat. — I drink tea with warm milk.)
Heißes Wasser ist gefährlich. (neuter, Nom. — Hot water is dangerous.)

title.en: Present participle used as an adjective

explanation.en:
The Partizip I represents an ongoing, active action. Form it using the infinitive + -d-. When used before a noun, add standard adjective endings.
Example: weinen -> ein weinendes Kind (a child that is currently crying).

rule.en:
Partizip I as an adjective
InfinitivePartizip Ias adjective
weinenweinendein weinendes Kind
schlafenschlafendein schlafendes Baby

Formation: infinitive + -d + regular adjective ending.

Meaning: the action is happening right now, actively, at the same time (= 'while it is X-ing').

Examples
Ein weinendes Kind braucht Trost. (= a child that is currently crying needs comfort)
Das schlafende Baby ist süß. (The sleeping baby is cute.)

title.en: Past participle used as an adjective

explanation.en:
The Partizip II (past participle) can be placed directly before a noun. It describes a completed or passive action and requires standard adjective endings.
Example: kochen -> gekocht -> ein gekochtes Ei (a boiled egg).

rule.en:
Partizip II as an adjective
InfinitivePartizip IIas adjective
kochengekochtein gekochtes Ei
schließengeschlossenein geschlossenes Fenster

Meaning: the action is already completed or happened passively (= 'the thing that has already been X-ed').

Examples
Ein gekochtes Ei zum Frühstück. (= an egg that has already been boiled. A boiled egg for breakfast.)
Das geschlossene Fenster war kalt. (The closed window was cold.)

Compare with Partizip I: weinendes Kind (active, happening now) vs. gekochtes Ei (passive, completed).

explanation.en:
A two-part connector used to express an alternative. You can only choose one of the two options available.
Example: Zum Frühstück trinke ich entweder Kaffee oder Tee.

rule.en:
entweder … oder (either … or)
ConnectorMeaning
entweder ... oderalternative: only one of two options is possible

Examples
Zum Frühstück trinke ich entweder Kaffee oder Tee. (not both — For breakfast I drink either coffee or tea.)
Wir fahren entweder nach Italien oder nach Spanien. (We're going either to Italy or to Spain.)

Word order: if entweder starts the sentence, the verb comes right after it (position 2): Entweder kommst du mit, oder du bleibst hier.

title.en: Sentence connectors: overview (und, oder, denn, deshalb, trotzdem, weil, dass, wenn, obwohl)

explanation.en: Comprehensive B1 overview of sentence connectors. We classify three types: 1) Position 0 (<g>und, aber, denn, oder</g>), 2) Main clause connectors at Position 1 (<g>deshalb, trotzdem</g> followed by verb), 3) Subordinate clause connectors (<g>weil, dass, wenn, obwohl</g> with verb at the end).

rule.en:
Sentence connectors — big overview
TypeConnectorsWord order
Position 0und, aber, denn, oderno change
Position 1deshalb, trotzdemverb comes right after (inversion)
Subordinate clauseweil, dass, wenn, obwohlverb at the end

Examples
Es regnet, aber ich gehe raus. (position 0)
Es regnet, deshalb bleibe ich hier. (position 1)
Ich bleibe hier, weil es regnet. (subordinate clause, verb at the end)

Tip: When in doubt, always ask: Does the connector change the normal word order? And if so — how?

title.en: Word formation: separable verbs with mit-/weg-/weiter-/zusammen-/zurück-

explanation.en:
Review of separable prefixes that move to the end of the sentence. Prefixes alter the core meaning: mit- (together), weg- (away), weiter- (continue), zurück- (back).
Example: Ich komme morgen mit. Wir arbeiten weiter.

rule.en:
Separable verbs with mit-, weg-, weiter-, zusammen-, zurück-
PrefixMeaning
mit-togetherness (along with others)
weg-away (away from here)
weiter-continuation (not stopping)
zusammen-togetherness, union
zurück-repetition, return

Word order: in the present/Präteritum, the prefix goes to the very end of the sentence, separated from the verb stem.

Examples
Ich komme morgen mit. (mitkommen — I'll come along tomorrow.)
Wir arbeiten weiter. (weiterarbeiten — We keep working.)
Er kommt nächste Woche zurück. (zurückkommen — He's coming back next week.)
